description: A equipe Stellari-Scientificᴁ, é formada por estudantes da rede de colégios Santa Maria Minas que buscam resolver problemas propostos pela NASA e desenvolver soluções inovadoras que auxiliem no progresso da sociedade como um todo. Todos os estudantes membros da equipe contam com foco na área de engenharia e ciência, assim como no desenvolvimento de pesquisa científica ao longo da vida estudantil.
summary: The Ignis project is an interface integrated with a wide range of sensors that have their information interpreted by an S.I and shown in an easy-to-understand panel. Using a probabilistic model created by the team, the S.I can predict the risk of fire incidents based on the data collected by the sensors. In addition to this, the PCB's inside the ring are totally designed and calculated by our crew to meet the demands of the chosen sensors and to maintain the quality and efficiency of our project. With this, we aim to contribute to the development of fire prevention technology.
details:
Ignis Project

1 - Introduction

The Ignis project introduces an integrated interface powered by a diverse array of sensors, whose data are interpreted by an Super Intelligence system and displayed on an intuitive, user-friendly dashboard. Utilizing a custom probabilistic model developed by the research team, the S.I is capable of predicting the risk of fire incidents based on real-time data collected by the sensor network.

Furthermore, the printed circuit boards used at the ring were meticulously designed and engineered by our team to meet the precise demands of the selected sensors, thereby ensuring the overall quality and operational efficiency of the system. Through this initiative, we aim to contribute significantly to the advancement of fire prevention technology.

2 - Smart - ONE (PCB's)

The Smart-ONE boards were designed as a custom two-layer printed circuit board (PCB) in KiCad.

Each board is built around an ATmega328P microcontroller clocked by a 16 MHz crystal and powered from a 5 V input through an AMS1117-3.3 linear regulator that supplies the 3.3 V logic rail. A CH340C USB-to-serial converter connects the microcontroller’s pins to the host computer, with DTR coupled to the reset line through a 100 nF capacitor to allow automatic reset during programming.

Six connectors (J1–J6) provide, respectively, USB and energy input, the analog gas-sensor interface, the I²C bus for the MPU6050 sensor, general-purpose I/O and reset, the touch input, and the serial link to the hub. After fabrication, the boards were assembled and validated electrically, including power-rail checks and continuity tests of the programming and sensor paths, before firmware was loaded through the USB bootloader.

Also, the GERBER archives from the fabrication are avaliable at our Git Hub repository.

https://github.com/bpacheco007/Ignis-Project---NASA-Space-Apps/blob/725ddf18445b2483cfb44966b757217eb3cfc918/BPSmartPlateONEFinalVersion.zip

And also a photo of the plate got attached before the placement of the eletronic components.

3 - The Ring

The ring is a five-sector structure in which each 72° segment houses is one module, the five segments together form a closed circular band around a central axis.

The ring has an intern radius of 46 mm, an extern radius of 68 mm, and a height of 52 mm, with a 2.4 mm wall. Four sectors hold one Smart ONE board each, each carrying a sensor mounted on its outer face, while the fifth sector holds the hub, which combines the MPU6050 inertial sensor, the MQ-8 gas sensor, the LDR light sensor, the NTC temperature sensor, and the Ra-02 LoRa radio.

Adjacent sectors join through matching ledges and notches on their ends, and M3 screws secured by heat-set inserts fix them together. Power enters the hub through the splitter, and the hub’s 3.3 V output supplies the boards, since the ring has no room for a USB-C connector. The hub streams its sensor readings to the host PC over USB, where the interface rotates the ring model according to the measured roll and pitch and computes the ignition risk index from the readings, so the physical ring and the digital display stay aligned in orientation.

Also a photo of the ring got attached before and after the placement of the eletronic components.

4 - The Interface

The interface is a web page that runs in Chrome or Edge and connects to the hub over USB through the Web Serial API at 115200 baud.

The hub sends one line every 500 ms containing the MPU6050 roll, pitch and gravity magnitude, plus the raw voltages of the MQ-8, LDR and NTC sensors. The interface converts these readings into engineering units: gravity in m/s², gas concentration in % vol, irradiance in W/m², and temperature in kelvin.

It then evaluates Equation (8) of the physicochemical model, using the constants from Table I, and displays the resulting ignition probability and the individual factors FG, FF, FT, FP and FE. Five status cards show whether the hub, each sensor and the MPU6050 are providing valid data, an overall status indicator summarizes the system, and a three-dimensional model of the ring, with its five coloured sectors, rotates in real time to follow the measured attitude of the ring.

Conclusion

We built a complete, working chain from the sensors on the ring to a physics-based risk display, using a modular ring design, low-cost sensors and open tools.

The model combines five factors, gravity, fuel concentration, temperature, pressure and irradiance, into a single ignition probability, and the interface makes that calculation visible and traceable. The work is still a prototype, however. The conversion curves for the gas, light and temperature sensors are estimates that must be calibrated against reference measurements, the MQ-8 measurement range is below the lower flammability limit used in the model, so it cannot yet show a non-zero probability on its own, and the pressure and oxygen fraction are fixed values because the ring has no sensors for them.

The next steps are calibration, adding sensors for pressure and oxygen, and validating the model experimentally, which is what would turn the prototype into a reliable tool for microgravity fire-safety assessment.
